Finalmente, pobrecito mancebo, si alguna buenaventura os ha de dar nuestro señor, si nuestro señor te tiene en algo, primero te conviene que experimentes trabajos y pobrezas y sufras fatigas intolerables, como se ofrecen a los que andan de pueblo en pueblo, que son grandes cansancios y grandes sudores y grandes fríos y grandes calores. Andaréis lleno de polvo; fatigaros ha el mecapal en la frente; iréis limpiando el sudor de la cara con las manos; augmentarse ha vuestro trabajo, en que seréis compelido a dormir al rincón y detrás de la puerta de casas ajenas, y allí estaréis cabizbaxo y avergonzado, y tendréis la barriga pegada a las costillas de hambre, y andaréis de pueblo en pueblo discorriendo. Y demás desto, os afligirá la duda de la venta de vuestras mercaderías, que por ventura no se venderán, y desto tendréis tristeza y lloro. Antes que alcancéis algún caudal o buenaventura, habéis de ser afligido y trabajado hasta lo último de potencia. Y allende desto, muchas veces os será necesario dormir en algu[na]

Finally, my poor little young man, if our lord should give you some good fortune, if our lord thinks anything of you, you should first experience hardships and misery, and suffer intolerable fatigue, such as those [hardships] that face those who drift from town to town; [hardships] which consist of great tiredness, profuse sweat, and intense cold and heat. You will walk covered in dust; the _mecapal_[^25] will tire your forehead. You will go about wiping sweat off your face with your hands. Your toil will be increased so that you will be compelled to sleep in a corner or behind the door in strange houses, where you will find yourself dejected and ashamed; and you will have your belly stuck to your ribs from hunger, and you will keep traveling from town to town. And besides all this, you will keep worrying about the sale of your merchandise, which perhaps will not be sold, and you will feel sad and shed tears because of this. Before you can earn any wealth or good fortune, you will be tormented and worked to the end of your strength. And beyond all this, often you will have to sleep in some 


[^25]: _mecapal_: the tumpline that was tied to the forehead and served to carry loads on the back of a porter. Here Sahagún Hispanicizes the Nahuatl noun _mecapalli_ to _mecapal_.

nahuatl_col.subtitle: (Anderson & Dibble 1953–1982)
nahuatl_col.html:
to danger and adversity. For not without reason did the merchants take and find leadership and the wisdom of old age, become leaders, and receive their authority in exchange.

“And of this, O poor youth, if something should be thy reward and deserts, if our lord should show esteem by something for thee, thou must first feel and profit by the pain, the afflictions, the privations, the ambushes. Such is exacted from those who go from city to city. Yet there will be times of need. Thou shalt become tired and worn out; thou shalt stand exhausted; thou shalt go wearied by heat, spent by winds. Thy face will become dust-covered and deathly white. Thy forehead will burn; thou shalt wipe the sweat off with thy hand; indeed thou shalt be bathed [in it]. In the corner, by the wall, behind the door, thou shalt hang thy head. Thy stomach will stick to thee [from hunger].1

“Thou shalt go into, entering, and leaving, city after city. Thou shalt be in danger; it will not be well with thee. That is to say, perchance it will not prosper; perhaps thy stock of goods, thy just deserts, thy dealings, will not result well. Thou shalt be long-suffering; thou shalt shed tears. Thy good deeds will not bear fruit, for fatigue will take thy measure. Indeed, thy breath and courage will end.2

“Perhaps somewhere in a gorge, at the mouth of a canyon, on some high place, at the base of a rock, at the foot of a tree, shalt thou sleep. Perchance somewhere thou shalt be destroyed;
